claims.text: Protective oxide development and retention in high-temperature HEAs is governed by preferential surface segregation of oxide-forming elements such as Al or Cr.
Surface-segregated Al or Cr forms stable, adherent protective oxide layers at high temperature.
The initial HEA is compositionally homogeneous and contains protective-oxide-forming elements such as Al, Cr, or Si.
The proposed oxidation exposure is conducted in air or an oxygen-rich atmosphere at 800–1200°C for 100 hours under controlled oxygen partial pressure.
High configurational entropy promotes a uniform distribution of elements in HEAs.
Under high-temperature oxidative conditions, elements with high oxygen affinity, such as Al and Cr, segregate to the alloy surface.
Surface-enriched Al and Cr form Al2O3 and Cr2O3, respectively.
The resulting Al- or Cr-rich oxides are dense and stable.
These oxide layers inhibit further oxidation by limiting oxygen diffusion.
These oxide layers inhibit further oxidation by limiting metal-ion diffusion.
HEAs with higher Al or Cr concentrations will develop more stable and adherent oxide layers than otherwise comparable HEAs with lower concentrations or without those elements.
HEAs with higher Al or Cr concentrations will exhibit lower oxidation mass gain than HEAs with lower concentrations or without those elements.
A conventional single-phase alloy, such as a Ni-based superalloy, can serve as a baseline under identical oxidation conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only to HEAs containing elements capable of forming protective oxides.
The proposed mechanism applies only under conditions in which the protective oxides are thermodynamically stable and does not apply in reducing environments.
Varying Al and Cr concentrations while holding oxidation conditions fixed can test whether their concentrations control mass gain and oxide-layer properties.
Mass gain, XPS oxide composition, and SEM oxide morphology can be used to evaluate the predicted oxidation response.
Failure of higher-Al or higher-Cr HEAs to show lower mass gain or stable, adherent oxides relative to lower-content HEAs or the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
